claims.text: A conformal ultrathin Ni coating can be deposited uniformly on W particles by methods such as chemical vapor deposition or electroplating.
Ni coating of W particles before Cu infiltration will improve W/Cu interfacial bonding.
Ni coating of W particles before Cu infiltration will reduce void formation relative to vapor-coated W powder processing.
Uncoated or vapor-coated W particles sintered with Cu exhibit phase separation and voids.
Phase separation and voids in these W–Cu composites impair thermal transport.
Processing near 1200 °C under reduced pressure or inert gas minimizes oxidation during W–Cu infiltration or sintering.
A Ni interlayer facilitates improved wetting between W and Cu.
A Ni interlayer facilitates diffusion bonding between W and Cu.
The Ni interlayer acts as a diffusion barrier that prevents interfacial reactions leading to void formation.
Ni lowers the interfacial energy between W and Cu.
Improved wetting and bonding promote more uniform interdiffusion and contact during infiltration or sintering.
More uniform interdiffusion and contact minimize void formation and phase separation.
The Ni layer stabilizes the W/Cu interface under irradiation.
Irradiation-induced interface stabilization by Ni preserves mechanical durability.
Relative to vapor-coated W powder followed by sintering, Ni-coated W will produce significantly lower void content.
Relative to vapor-coated W powder followed by sintering, Ni-coated W will produce higher thermal conductivity.
Relative to vapor-coated W powder followed by sintering, Ni-coated W will maintain or improve mechanical durability under irradiation.
Vapor coating followed by sintering, spark-plasma sintering, and mechanical alloying suffer from residual voids and imperfect W/Cu interfacial contact.
Ni may diffuse into Cu or W during prolonged irradiation and thereby modify interfacial properties.

contradictions.description: The proposed processing and experiment use approximately 1200 °C, while the stated applicability boundary specifies sub-1200 °C processing; whether the planned experiment lies inside the claimed boundary is therefore ambiguous.
